title: An AI trading tool for beginners
author: GemeriCorp
selftext:
NOTE: Just wanted to share a tool I built and use myself to filter trades. Mainly looking for feedback or to help people having issues when getting into trading

About 2 years ago, while learning to trade, I was pretty much trying every strategy I could find. And for some reason, thinking I was a genius, I jumped straight into live trading, which ended in me watching my portfolio collapse

After that, I went back to paper trading while learning ML and AI trading, and eventually started building something I wish I'd had when I first started

It's not an AI that picks stocks or strategies for you. Instead, it helps you evaluate trades you're already considering

Basically, you enter a ticker, choose BUY, SELL, or NONE, and get two things, the trade filter that scores your trade from 0–100 based on how favorable the setup looks and the market timer that gives a WAIT or EXECUTE verdict based on current entry timing

The system used to compute these scores arent LLMs but are instead ML models similar to what quants would use, while the score reasoning and chart analysis are instead generated by AI to turn the complicated code outputs into normal readable language

One thing that always frustrated me about AI trading tools was how many just spit out tickers or without explanation. With this tool, however, you keep the autonomy. It doesn't replace you as the trader, and you still need to find your own strategies

Obviously, it's not perfect, and I'm not claiming it's some magic money printer. It's just something I wish I'd had when I started trading. However for those of you who may be reasonably skeptical, I put together an evidence showing walk-foward historical simulations across 30 tickers

You can try it here: [https://sentinelscores.com](https://sentinelscores.com/)   
or find the evidence page here: [https://sentinelscores.com/evidence](https://sentinelscores.com/evidence)

I've made sure that the evidence page is completely open and transparent. It's completely free, and you can use a guest account. If anyone wants to run a few trades through it and share what works, what doesn't, or what you'd want added, I'd really appreciate it

Thanks, and happy to answer questions!

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body: a 0 to 100 score is only worth something if it's calibrated. have you checked whether the trades it scored 70+ actually did better than the ones it scored 40, on your own paper history?

replies.author: GemeriCorp
replies.body:
Yes. on average over 1 trading year, scores being 70+ had average returns around 3–5 percentage points higher than those scoring between 50–69

Trades above 80 also showed roughly a 12-percentage-point higher win rate compared to those below 80

In the end, the 0–100 score measures the strength of evidence supporting an action, acting as a confidence score not profit possibility

Do you think I should add this information to the evidence page?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: that's a better answer than most tools give. one year is where I'd be careful: a single year is mostly one kind of market, so I'd split it by quarter and see if the 70+ gap holds in the down stretches or only the up ones.

replies.author: GemeriCorp
replies.body:
Just ran that test, and the 70+ gap actually held up in 4/5 quarters, with average returns being 2–7 percentage points higher than trades scoring 50–69. Across all five quarters, the average gap was around 3 percentage points

In the one quarter where it didn't hold up, trades scoring 50–69 actually outperformed 70+ by about 1 percentage point

The overall mean trade return was also positive in every quarter. The total trade sample for the trading year was 642 which isnt a small size but still would be better with more examples of different market regimes. Still interesting to see the gap mostly holding up

Although maybe for a more in-depth backtest I'll have to give Quantradin a try :)

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: 4 of 5 quarters is better than I expected for a single score. the quarter that broke is the one I'd look at hardest: if it was a falling quarter, the score is mostly reading trend strength, which is fine, but a beginner seeing a 75 in a selloff should know that.

replies.author: GemeriCorp
replies.body:
That's a good point. I looked into the quarter where the gap reversed, and there were actually very few trades scoring above 70, with most falling between 50–69. My suspicion is that the choppier market conditions increased uncertainty, which pushed scores lower overall. Because there were so few 70+ trades, their average return was also more sensitive to individual outcomes, which could explain the 1-percentage-point difference  
  
I definitely agree that showing how the score behaves across different market regimes would be useful, especially for beginners

replies.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
replies.body: Yes, add it, and show the trade count in each score bucket and the out-of-sample version next to it, so a reader can see how much weight the 3 to 5 point difference deserves

comments.author: TastyTrading
comments.body: I use ThetaPal AI market scouts

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: Showing the walk-forward results with the losing tickers included is the right level of openness, and the “beat buy and hold 13 of 30” line is an honest figure to display. One thing I’d add is the breakdown that readers can’t see yet: the calibration table (average result by score bucket, with the number of trades in each) and the same table on a period the models weren’t trained on, since a 12-point win-rate gap from one year of data can shrink once samples are separated. A beginner-facing tool also benefits from showing the worst outcome next to the average, as you do with drawdown. Backtest Labs at Cymetica is one place to see how strategy results get compared against buy and hold.
